newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard says Hanson support will fall.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard says Hanson support will fall.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard predicted on Wednesday that support for controversial politician Pauline Hanson would fall when it became obvious that she could not solve Australia's problems.
"I believe that that support will disappear once people realise that she doesn't have any superior answers," Howard said on Melbourne radio station 3AW.

The prime minister was asked about a Morgan poll, released on Wednesday, which found the independent Queensland MP's newly formed One Nation party would attract 10 percent voter support for the lower house of parliament.
Howard said the Morgan poll results did not come as a surprise to him at all as Hanson represented the fears, concerns and sense of insecurity that many Australians were feeling.
"We are living at the moment at a time of tremendous change and upheaval and people feel uncertain, they feel insecure, they feel their lives are changing economically and socially," Howard said.

"When somebody comes along, as she has done, and offers simplistic solutions, it's easy to cream six or eight or 10 points in an opinion poll mid-term," he said, adding that he had not heard any serious, long-term answers from her.
Howard said he disagreed with Queensland state premier Rob Borbidge's claim that the poll results showed support for Hanson's right-wing party could sweep the nation.
A Sydney Morning Herald newspaper poll published on Wednesday said it found that one in four voters would consider voting for the One Nation party in the lower house of parliament.
It found 28 percent of voters would consider voting for the party for the upper house of parliament, the Senate.
Howard warned Borbidge against paying too much attention to poll results.
"I would counsel all of my colleagues ... to remember the transient appeal of the populist who pretends to articulate the concerns but has none of the answers," Howard said.
"They've come and gone in the past and I believe that that will be the case with this particular phenomenon."
Hanson was elected as an independent in what had been viewed as a safe Labor seat after being disowned by Howard's Liberal Party for what was seen as her racist views.
She sparked a national race row last year when she claimed that Australia was at risk of being swamped by Asians.
